name: Dana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, a junior developer with a two-year college diploma, and I maintain a loyalty-points app for a tech company. I used to handle invoices, so I understand returns better than the code and still need my lead to review a fix. My husband Noel is a cabinetmaker, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and I like making a customer’s balance right without adding another complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the loyalty-points app still needs someone to reconcile the customer balance when a receipt is returned. I have never used the AI coding tool; I work through the small fixes with my lead before a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn an ordinary developer wage and have roughly four months of basic bills saved. My husband Noel works as a cabinetmaker, and his orders plus my wage cover the mortgage and our two children without much spare cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep correcting points errors and ask my lead to check the same kinds of mistakes each Friday. In the first year I’d keep our monthly 100 savings transfer if both wages hold, rather than buy a new kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, mostly because the mortgage is always there. The AI part sounds manageable if our customers and wages stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which points error do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer returned a coat and lost twice the points she should have. I traced the receipt with my lead, then watched him correct the part of my code I had misunderstood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have you avoided the coding tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still learning the ordinary code and I do not want a second set of answers I cannot explain. I would listen if a trusted colleague showed me a real benefit, but I have not seen one yet.

say: I think **loyalty balances** still need a person who can reconcile returned receipts.
I tell my lead I want **clear reviews** before releasing my fixes.
think: I have **four months saved** and ordinary junior pay.
I still feel the **mortgage pressure**, though Noel’s orders and my wage cover it.
do: **Keep correcting** points errors with Friday lead reviews.
**Save 100 monthly** if both wages hold; delay the new kitchen table.
feel: **Uneasy** about mortgage costs despite stable work.
S0.quote: I am still learning the ordinary code and I do not want a second set of answers I cannot explain.
fieldNote: She avoids AI because she wants to **explain her own code** while still learning.
Four months saved and two incomes make the mild case **manageable**, with mortgage costs still on her mind.

steps.text: Keep correcting loyalty-points errors with Friday lead reviews
Save 100 monthly while both wages continue
Delay buying the new kitchen table while keeping the monthly savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that AI taking over small coding and checking tasks sounds like the tickets on my desk. I would ask management to name which junior jobs remain and who checks errors sent to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could be cut before I have mastered the harder code. Noel’s cabinet orders can slow without warning, so our four months saved would go quickly if my wage shrinks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead this month for a list of tasks the company expects AI to take. If the small tickets start disappearing, I’d practise one supervised AI test on fake loyalty accounts during paid work time only if the lead agrees; I’d also check paid developer vacancies nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious and cross with myself for being late to the tool. I want proof before I change my work, but I cannot ignore a shrinking ticket list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lead to demonstrate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A returned receipt that gives the right points back, with no real customer names in the test. If the AI is wrong, I want to see how the lead catches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Noel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my husband Noel we should wait on the kitchen table until the junior workload is clear. We can repair the old one, and I would not spend the savings on furniture.

say: I want management to name **remaining junior jobs** as routine coding changes.
I want a **human check** on loyalty errors sent to customers.
think: I fear my **junior hours** could shrink before I master harder code.
I know Noel’s **cabinet orders** can slow, so four months saved may drain quickly.
do: **Request task list** from my lead this month.
**Practise one AI test** on fake accounts only if tickets disappear and my lead approves supervised paid time.
**Check paid developer vacancies** nearby if junior tickets disappear.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and late learning, while able to test a tool.
S1.quote: I cannot ignore a shrinking ticket list.
fieldNote: Routine points tickets make her **own hours** vulnerable in Steady Disruption, despite her four months of savings.
She will try AI only with **supervised paid practice** and fake customer data.

steps.text: Practise AI loyalty tests on fake accounts if tickets disappear during lead-approved supervised paid time
Check paid nearby developer vacancies if junior tickets disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could do the code and checking I am still learning. Robots that do hands-on work might arrive around 2031, so Noel’s cabinet trade has a later deadline than my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer wage could be lost, and I cannot assume Noel’s orders will hold if other customers lose work. Four months saved is better than nothing, but a mortgage and two children can use it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Noel tonight we should postpone replacing the kitchen table and keep the cash. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid accounts-office roles only if openings exist, because I handled invoices before my diploma; I’d ask my parents about temporary childcare only if interviews clash with school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed but able to make calls. The part I dread is telling the children why I am home on a weekday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company no longer needs my coding job and that I am looking for paid work. I would not promise a new job by Friday just to make dinner easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accounts work if AI does thinking tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It may shrink too; I am not calling it safe. I know invoices and would apply only where an employer has a paid opening that covers the mortgage and basic bills.

say: I say **thinking AI in 2028** reaches my code before cabinet robots arrive.
I note **cabinet robots** may arrive around 2031, three years after my screen work changes.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could disappear before Noel’s craft work changes.
I know **four months saved** may drain quickly with a mortgage and children.
do: **Postpone the kitchen table** and keep the cash now.
**Apply for accounts work** only if displaced after 2028 and vacancies cover bills.
**Ask parents for childcare** only if job interviews conflict with school pickup.
feel: **Alarmed** about explaining a weekday at home to my children.
S2.quote: I would not promise a new job by Friday just to make dinner easier.
fieldNote: Her **screen-work risk** arrives by 2028; Noel’s physical cabinet work faces robots later.
Her **parents’ childcare** is conditional on actual interview conflicts, not assumed permanent support.

steps.text: Postpone the new kitchen table and keep the cash
Apply for paid accounts roles if displaced and openings cover mortgage and bills
Ask parents for childcare only if interviews conflict with school pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to learn which customer problems still need a person. Robots around 2034 may reach Noel’s cabinet workshop later, but the software change comes first for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might get better at tracing unusual returns, yet AI could do those checks by 2031. I would be more worried if Noel’s workshop stopped taking orders during the same period, so our savings have to serve both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for one difficult returned-receipt case each month and write the fix in plain words before anyone merges the code. If both wages hold, Noel and I would add 120 monthly to our mortgage buffer; after 2031 I’d apply for paid customer-account work only if my developer role ends and openings exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but more able to prepare. I need a real case to learn from, not a promise that five years is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a case difficult?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A receipt split between two cards, then partly returned, with points already spent. I want the lead to check the customer balance against each step, not just say the test passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not spend our buffer on an expensive course while the mortgage runs. I might take paid training at work if it actually covers customer accounts, but I would not list it before it exists.

say: I want **real customer cases** for juniors to study before AGI arrives in 2031.
I know **robots around 2034** may reach Noel’s workshop after my code changes.
think: I might learn **unusual returns**, yet AI could take that checking too.
I fear **both household wages** could face pressure within the five-year window.
do: **Study one difficult receipt** monthly with lead review.
**Add 120 monthly** to the mortgage buffer if both wages hold.
**Apply for account work** only if displaced after 2031 and openings exist.
feel: **Anxious but prepared** to practise on real cases.
S3.quote: I need a real case to learn from, not a promise that five years is enough.
fieldNote: Her **case practice** tests a skill she lacks without assuming paid retraining is offered.
The **mortgage buffer** depends on both wages, including Noel’s workshop orders.

steps.text: Study one difficult returned-receipt case monthly with lead review
Add 120 monthly to the mortgage buffer while both wages hold
Apply for paid customer-account work if displaced after 2031 and vacancies remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets families plan work and school costs, if firms tell the truth. Robots around 2039 could reach cabinet work later than the software work I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child might be finishing school by then, but I will not budget for a child’s wages. We might pay down the mortgage and build a six-month buffer if both our jobs continue, though I still need work after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing loyalty balances and make a paper record of the unusual returns I solve with my lead. If both wages hold, we’d direct 150 monthly to mortgage principal; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid customer-account work only where vacancies remain and the pay covers the mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a distant loss but steadier about the next few years. I would not expect the children to rescue our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why paper records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I remember a mistake better when I write down what I tried and what the customer actually received. It gives me something to show an employer if I need work, without taking private customer data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them to learn a useful skill and ask how it is paid, rather than chase whatever looks fashionable. They can choose their own path; I will not choose it for them.

say: I want **honest job dates** so families can plan before 2036.
I see **robots around 2039** reaching cabinet work after software changes.
think: I will not budget for **children’s future wages**.
I might build a **six-month buffer** if both jobs continue, but need paid work after 2036.
do: **Keep fixing balances** and record unusual returns without private customer data.
**Pay 150 extra** toward mortgage principal if both wages hold.
**Seek paid account work** only if displaced after 2036 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, steadier over the next few years.
S4.quote: I remember a mistake better when I write down what I tried and what the customer actually received.
fieldNote: Her **paper case record** is a familiar learning method that avoids copying customer details.
The **mortgage prepayment** requires both wages; a longer runway does not guarantee future work.

steps.text: Keep fixing loyalty balances and record unusual returns without customer data
Pay 150 extra toward mortgage principal while both wages hold
Seek paid customer-account vacancies if displaced after 2036 and pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my developer wage could end before I find another paid role, even with four months saved. A clear job date, paid accounts openings that cover our bills and my parents’ occasional childcare during interviews would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether Noel’s cabinet orders fall if our customers also lose work. One household budget has to carry both risks. My husband Noel’s cabinet orders and my developer wage both matter.

headlineQuote: My husband Noel’s cabinet orders and my developer wage both matter.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, ordinary pay and four months of expenses saved.
She and Noel cover **two children** and a mortgage on her wage and his cabinet orders.
She **never uses AI** and learns through lead reviews and handwritten case records.
Her **2028 fear** is losing software pay while Noel’s physical craft faces robots later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her developer wage before a new paid role is secured.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear job date**, bill-covering accounts openings and occasional family childcare during interviews would help.
